request.user:
[2020 summer phd math-stat — problem 1]

Suppose $(Y_1, \dots, Y_n)$ are observed, where $Y_i = \max(0, X_i)$ and $(X_1, \dots, X_n)$ are i.i.d. $N(\mu^*, \sigma^{*2})$ with $(\mu^*, \sigma^*)$ unknown. Define $R_i = \mathbb{1}\{Y_i > 0\}$. Let $\Phi(\cdot)$ be the $N(0,1)$ CDF. For $\theta = (\beta, \sigma)$ with $\beta = \mu/\sigma$, let $P_\theta$ denote $N(\mu, \sigma^2)$, and $\theta^* = (\beta^*, \sigma^*)$.
(i) Define an estimator $\hat\theta_1 = (\hat\beta_1, \hat\sigma_1)$ as the solution of $\mathbb{E}_\theta(R_1) = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n R_i$ and $\mathbb{E}_\theta(R_1 Y_1) = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n R_i Y_i$. Find closed-form expressions for $(\hat\beta_1, \hat\sigma_1)$ (you may use $\Phi$ and its inverse).
(ii) Show that $(\hat\beta_1, \hat\sigma_1)$ are consistent estimators of $(\beta^*, \sigma^*)$.
(iii) Show that $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta_1 - \theta^*) \xrightarrow{D} N(0, \tau_1)$ for some variance $\tau_1$; find a closed-form expression for $\tau_1$.
(iv) Write down the log-likelihood $\ell(\theta)$, and compute $\mathbb{E}_\theta\{\frac1n \frac{\partial \ell(\theta)}{\partial \theta}\}$ and $n\operatorname{var}_\theta\{\frac1n \frac{\partial \ell(\theta)}{\partial \theta}\}$ in closed form.
(v) The MLE $\hat\theta_2 = (\hat\beta_2, \hat\sigma_2)$ satisfies $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta_2 - \theta^*) \xrightarrow{D} N(0, \tau_2)$ (you need not prove this). Find a closed-form expression for $\tau_2$.
(vi) Show that $\tau_1 \ge \tau_2$. Give a direct proof, instead of invoking the asymptotic efficiency of maximum likelihood estimation.

Let \(\phi=\Phi'\) denote the standard normal density. Write
\[
X=\sigma(Z+\beta),\qquad Z\sim N(0,1),
\]
so that
\[
R=\mathbf 1\{X>0\}=\mathbf 1\{Z>-\beta\}.
\]

For shorthand, for a fixed \(\beta\), define
\[
p=\Phi(\beta),\qquad c=1-p=\Phi(-\beta),\qquad q=\phi(\beta),
\]
and
\[
G=\beta p+q.
\]

---

## (i) Closed form for \((\hat\beta_1,\hat\sigma_1)\)

We have
\[
\mathbb E_\theta(R_1)=P_\theta(X_1>0)=P(Z>-\beta)=\Phi(\beta)=p.
\]
Also,
\[
\mathbb E_\theta(R_1Y_1)
=\mathbb E_\theta\{X_1\mathbf 1(X_1>0)\}
=\sigma \mathbb E\{(Z+\beta)\mathbf 1(Z>-\beta)\}.
\]
Now
\[
\mathbb E\{Z\mathbf 1(Z>-\beta)\}=\phi(\beta)=q,
\]
so
\[
\mathbb E_\theta(R_1Y_1)
=\sigma\{\beta\Phi(\beta)+\phi(\beta)\}
=\sigma G.
\]

Let
\[
\bar R_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n R_i,\qquad 
\bar W_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n R_iY_i.
\]
The estimating equations are
\[
\Phi(\beta)=\bar R_n,\qquad 
\sigma\{\beta\Phi(\beta)+\phi(\beta)\}=\bar W_n.
\]
Thus, on the event \(0<\bar R_n<1\),
\[
\boxed{\hat\beta_1=\Phi^{-1}(\bar R_n)}
\]
and
\[
\boxed{
\hat\sigma_1
=
\frac{\bar W_n}
{\hat\beta_1\bar R_n+\phi(\hat\beta_1)}
=
\frac{\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n R_iY_i}
{\Phi^{-1}(\bar R_n)\bar R_n+\phi(\Phi^{-1}(\bar R_n))}
}.
\]

If \(\bar R_n\in\{0,1\}\), no finite solution exists. Since under the model \(0<\Phi(\beta^*)<1\), this event has probability tending to \(0\), so it is asymptotically irrelevant.

---

## (ii) Consistency of \((\hat\beta_1,\hat\sigma_1)\)

Let
\[
p^*=\Phi(\beta^*),\qquad q^*=\phi(\beta^*),\qquad 
G^*=\beta^*p^*+q^*.
\]
By the Strong Law of Large Numbers,
\[
\bar R_n \xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}} p^*
\]
and
\[
\bar W_n
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n R_iY_i
\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}
\mathbb E_{\theta^*}(R_1Y_1)
=
\sigma^*G^*.
\]
Since \(p^*\in(0,1)\) and \(\Phi^{-1}\) is continuous on \((0,1)\),
\[
\hat\beta_1=\Phi^{-1}(\bar R_n)
\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}
\Phi^{-1}(p^*)=\beta^*.
\]
Also, the function \(G(\beta)=\beta\Phi(\beta)+\phi(\beta)\) is positive and continuous for all \(\beta\). Hence
\[
\hat\sigma_1
=
\frac{\bar W_n}{G(\hat\beta_1)}
\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}
\frac{\sigma^*G^*}{G^*}
=
\sigma^*.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{(\hat\beta_1,\hat\sigma_1)\xrightarrow{p}(\beta^*,\sigma^*)}.
\]

---

## (iii) Asymptotic distribution of \(\hat\theta_1\)

Let
\[
W_i=R_iY_i.
\]
At the true parameter \(\theta^*=(\beta^*,\sigma^*)\), write
\[
b=\beta^*,\qquad s=\sigma^*,
\]
and define
\[
p=\Phi(b),\qquad c=1-p,\qquad q=\phi(b),\qquad 
G=bp+q,
\]
and
\[
K=(1+b^2)p+bq.
\]

We have
\[
\mathbb E(R)=p,\qquad \mathbb E(W)=sG.
\]
Also,
\[
\operatorname{var}(R)=pc,
\]
\[
\operatorname{cov}(R,W)
=
\mathbb E(W)-\mathbb E(R)\mathbb E(W)
=
sG(1-p)=sGc,
\]
and
\[
\mathbb E(W^2)
=
s^2\mathbb E\{(Z+b)^2\mathbf 1(Z>-b)\}
=
s^2K.
\]
Thus
\[
V:=\operatorname{var}\begin{pmatrix}R\\ W\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
pc & sGc\\
sGc & s^2(K-G^2)
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

The moment map is
\[
m(\beta,\sigma)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\Phi(\beta)\\
\sigma\{\beta\Phi(\beta)+\phi(\beta)\}
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
p\\
\sigma G
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Since \(G'(\beta)=\Phi(\beta)=p\),
\[
D:=\frac{\partial m}{\partial(\beta,\sigma)}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
q & 0\\
sp & G
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Hence
\[
D^{-1}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
1/q & 0\\
-sp/(qG) & 1/G
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

By the multivariate Central Limit Theorem and the Delta Method,
\[
\sqrt n(\hat\theta_1-\theta^*)
\xrightarrow{D}
N(0,\tau_1),
\]
where
\[
\boxed{
\tau_1=D^{-1}VD^{-T}.
}
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\boxed{
\tau_1
=
\begin{pmatrix}
1/q & 0\\
-sp/(qG) & 1/G
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
pc & sGc\\
sGc & s^2(K-G^2)
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
1/q & -sp/(qG)\\
0 & 1/G
\end{pmatrix}.
}
\]

Writing the entries explicitly,
\[
\boxed{
\tau_{1,11}=\frac{pc}{q^2},
}
\]
\[
\boxed{
\tau_{1,12}=\tau_{1,21}
=
\frac{s\,c(qG-p^2)}{q^2G},
}
\]
and
\[
\boxed{
\tau_{1,22}
=
\frac{s^2}{G^2}
\left[
K-G^2-\frac{2pcG}{q}+\frac{p^3c}{q^2}
\right].
}
\]

---

## (iv) Log-likelihood, expected score, and score variance

The observed distribution of \(Y\) has an atom at \(0\) with mass
\[
P_\theta(Y=0)=P_\theta(X\le 0)=\Phi(-\beta)=c,
\]
and for \(y>0\), density
\[
f_\theta(y)=\frac1\sigma \phi\left(\frac y\sigma-\beta\right).
\]

Therefore the log-likelihood is
\[
\boxed{
\ell(\theta)
=
\sum_{i=1}^n
\left[
(1-R_i)\log \Phi(-\beta)
+
R_i\left\{
-\log\sigma+\log\phi\left(\frac{Y_i}{\sigma}-\beta\right)
\right\}
\right].
}
\]

Let
\[
T_i=\frac{Y_i}{\sigma}-\beta.
\]
The score for one observation is
\[
S_\beta(Y_i)
=
\frac{\partial \ell_i}{\partial\beta}
=
R_iT_i-(1-R_i)\frac{q}{c},
\]
and
\[
S_\sigma(Y_i)
=
\frac{\partial \ell_i}{\partial\sigma}
=
\frac{R_i}{\sigma}\left(T_i^2+\beta T_i-1\right).
\]

Thus
\[
\frac1n\frac{\partial\ell(\theta)}{\partial\theta}
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\begin{pmatrix}
S_\beta(Y_i)\\
S_\sigma(Y_i)
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Using the standard truncated-normal moments
\[
\mathbb E\{Z\mathbf 1(Z>-\beta)\}=q,
\]
\[
\mathbb E\{Z^2\mathbf 1(Z>-\beta)\}=p-\beta q,
\]
\[
\mathbb E\{Z^3\mathbf 1(Z>-\beta)\}=(\beta^2+2)q,
\]
one obtains
\[
\boxed{
\mathbb E_\theta\left\{
\frac1n\frac{\partial\ell(\theta)}{\partial\theta}
\right\}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
0\\
0
\end{pmatrix}.
}
\]

Now define
\[
A=p-\beta q+\frac{q^2}{c},
\]
and
\[
H=(\beta^2+2)p+\beta q.
\]
Then the variance of the one-observation score is
\[
I(\theta)
=
\operatorname{var}_\theta
\begin{pmatrix}
S_\beta(Y)\\
S_\sigma(Y)
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
A & G/\sigma\\
G/\sigma & H/\sigma^2
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Since the observations are i.i.d.,
\[
\boxed{
n\operatorname{var}_\theta\left\{
\frac1n\frac{\partial\ell(\theta)}{\partial\theta}
\right\}
=
I(\theta)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
p-\beta q+\dfrac{q^2}{c} & \dfrac{G}{\sigma}\\[1.2em]
\dfrac{G}{\sigma} & \dfrac{(\beta^2+2)p+\beta q}{\sigma^2}
\end{pmatrix}.
}
\]

---

## (v) Closed form for \(\tau_2\)

The MLE has asymptotic covariance equal to the inverse Fisher information matrix. Therefore
\[
\tau_2=I(\theta^*)^{-1}.
\]

At \(\theta^*=(b,s)\), define
\[
p=\Phi(b),\qquad c=1-p,\qquad q=\phi(b),
\]
\[
G=bp+q,
\]
\[
A=p-bq+\frac{q^2}{c},
\]
and
\[
H=(b^2+2)p+bq.
\]
Then
\[
I(\theta^*)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
A & G/s\\
G/s & H/s^2
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{
\tau_2
=
I(\theta^*)^{-1}
=
\frac{1}{AH-G^2}
\begin{pmatrix}
H & -sG\\
-sG & s^2A
\end{pmatrix}.
}
\]

---

## (vi) Direct proof that \(\tau_1\ge \tau_2\)

Here \(\tau_1\ge \tau_2\) means that \(\tau_1-\tau_2\) is positive semidefinite.

Let
\[
f(Y)=
\begin{pmatrix}
R\\
RY
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad 
m(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta f(Y).
\]
Let
\[
V=\operatorname{var}_{\theta^*}\{f(Y)\},
\]
and let
\[
S(Y;\theta)=\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\log p_\theta(Y)
\]
be the score. Also let
\[
I=I(\theta^*)=\operatorname{var}_{\theta^*}\{S(Y;\theta^*)\}.
\]

From part (iii),
\[
\tau_1=D^{-1}VD^{-T},
\]
where
\[
D=\frac{\partial m}{\partial\theta}\bigg|_{\theta=\theta^*}.
\]
From part (v),
\[
\tau_2=I^{-1}.
\]

Now, by differentiating under the integral sign,
\[
D
=
\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\mathbb E_\theta f(Y)\bigg|_{\theta=\theta^*}
=
\mathbb E_{\theta^*}\{f(Y)S(Y;\theta^*)^T\}.
\]
Since \(\mathbb E_{\theta^*}S(Y;\theta^*)=0\), this is
\[
D=\operatorname{cov}_{\theta^*}\{f(Y),S(Y;\theta^*)\}.
\]

Therefore the block covariance matrix
\[
\operatorname{var}_{\theta^*}
\begin{pmatrix}
f(Y)\\
S(Y;\theta^*)
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
V & D\\
D^T & I
\end{pmatrix}
\]
is positive semidefinite. Taking the Schur complement of \(I\), we get
\[
V-DI^{-1}D^T\ge 0.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\tau_1-\tau_2
=
D^{-1}VD^{-T}-I^{-1}
=
D^{-1}\{V-DI^{-1}D^T\}D^{-T}\ge 0.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{\tau_1\ge \tau_2.}
\]

This proves the inequality directly by a covariance/Schur-complement argument, without invoking asymptotic efficiency of the MLE.

\right\}
=
I(\theta)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
p-\beta q+\dfrac{q^2}{c} & \dfrac{G}{\sigma}\\[1.2em]
\dfrac{G}{\sigma} & \dfrac{(\beta^2+2)p+\beta q}{\sigma^2}
\end{pmatrix}.
}
\]

---

## (v) Closed form for \(\tau_2\)

The MLE has asymptotic covariance equal to the inverse Fisher information matrix. Therefore
\[
\tau_2=I(\theta^*)^{-1}.
\]

At \(\theta^*=(b,s)\), define
\[
p=\Phi(b),\qquad c=1-p,\qquad q=\phi(b),
\]
\[
G=bp+q,
\]
\[
A=p-bq+\frac{q^2}{c},
\]
and
\[
H=(b^2+2)p+bq.
\]
Then
\[
I(\theta^*)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
A & G/s\\
G/s & H/s^2
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{
\tau_2
=
I(\theta^*)^{-1}
=
\frac{1}{AH-G^2}
\begin{pmatrix}
H & -sG\\
-sG & s^2A
\end{pmatrix}.
}
\]

---

## (vi) Direct proof that \(\tau_1\ge \tau_2\)

Here \(\tau_1\ge \tau_2\) means that \(\tau_1-\tau_2\) is positive semidefinite.

Let
\[
f(Y)=
\begin{pmatrix}
R\\
RY
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad 
m(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta f(Y).
\]
Let
\[
V=\operatorname{var}_{\theta^*}\{f(Y)\},
\]
and let
\[
S(Y;\theta)=\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\log p_\theta(Y)
\]
be the score. Also let
\[
I=I(\theta^*)=\operatorname{var}_{\theta^*}\{S(Y;\theta^*)\}.
\]

From part (iii),
\[
\tau_1=D^{-1}VD^{-T},
\]
where
\[
D=\frac{\partial m}{\partial\theta}\bigg|_{\theta=\theta^*}.
\]
From part (v),
\[
\tau_2=I^{-1}.
\]

Now, by differentiating under the integral sign,
\[
D
=
\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\mathbb E_\theta f(Y)\bigg|_{\theta=\theta^*}
=
\mathbb E_{\theta^*}\{f(Y)S(Y;\theta^*)^T\}.
\]
Since \(\mathbb E_{\theta^*}S(Y;\theta^*)=0\), this is
\[
D=\operatorname{cov}_{\theta^*}\{f(Y),S(Y;\theta^*)\}.
\]

Therefore the block covariance matrix
\[
\operatorname{var}_{\theta^*}
\begin{pmatrix}
f(Y)\\
S(Y;\theta^*)
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
V & D\\
D^T & I
\end{pmatrix}
\]
is positive semidefinite. Taking the Schur complement of \(I\), we get
\[
V-DI^{-1}D^T\ge 0.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\tau_1-\tau_2
=
D^{-1}VD^{-T}-I^{-1}
=
D^{-1}\{V-DI^{-1}D^T\}D^{-T}\ge 0.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{\tau_1\ge \tau_2.}
\]

This proves the inequality directly by a covariance/Schur-complement argument, without invoking asymptotic efficiency of the MLE.
